entries.answer: A program in Filipino is a programa, and like most of the technical vocabulary the word is a direct English loan used in a Filipino sentence without any change. What is interesting about the word is that it covers two things English separates: the instructions themselves, and the scheduled television or radio show. A programmer writing about a program means the first, while a person discussing what they watched last night means the second, and a beginner who reads a sentence about a program being broadcast will not notice the ambiguity at all because the words are identical. The related terms are borrowed the same way, and a Filipino developer will say a function, an array or a variable rather than translate any of them, because a translated term would be less clear, not more. The one native alternative that does exist, and is now uncommon, is the older word for a written formula or programme of instructions in the sense of a schedule.

entries.answer: A programmer in Filipino is a programmer, and the role is described in English almost everywhere it is discussed, which is normal for the field. The word covers everyone who writes code, from a hobbyist to a professional, and it does not distinguish seniority the way a job title does, so a lead engineer and a junior developer are both simply a programmer unless a title is used. The related task words are also borrowed, and a developer is the term now used in job listings while a programmer remains the general word. A person who fixes other people's code rather than writing new code is described separately, as a person who debugs, which is a different job and one that grew out of the growth in size of codebases rather than out of any change in the work itself. What a programmer actually spends time on is rarely writing new code: reading existing code, working out why something failed, and testing are the majority of the day.
